meta.titre: Work Done by a Force: scalar product, slopes and the work-energy principle

source.epreuve_titre: GCE A/L Pure Mathematics with Mechanics past paper (Cameroon)

sections.contenu_markdown: A porter at a market in Douala lifts a sack of rice onto his head and then walks across the yard. In everyday language he works hard in both cases, but in mechanics only the force component along the direction of motion does work: carrying the sack horizontally at constant speed transfers no energy to the sack, while lifting it does. Work, defined as a scalar product of force and displacement, turns this idea into a number measured in joules. At Advanced Level the same definition appears with force and position vectors, on slopes, and in problems where the position of a particle is given as a function of time.

items: The scalar product of $\mathbf a=a_1\mathbf i+a_2\mathbf j+a_3\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=b_1\mathbf i+b_2\mathbf j+b_3\mathbf k$ is $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\cos\theta$.
Velocity is $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}$ and acceleration is $\mathbf a=\dfrac{d\mathbf v}{dt}$, found by differentiating each component.
Newton's second law: the resultant force on a particle of mass $m$ is $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$.
Kinetic energy is $\frac12mv^2$ and the weight of a mass $m$ is $mg$ with $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

sections.titre: Work as a scalar product, and work by a variable force
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Work done by a constant force
When a force $\mathbf F$ acts on a particle whose point of application undergoes a displacement $\mathbf d$, the work done by the force is the scalar product

$$
W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=|\mathbf F||\mathbf d|\cos\theta \tag{1}
$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf d$. Work is a scalar, measured in joules (J), where $1\ \mathrm{J}=1\ \mathrm{N\,m}$. With components, $W=F_1d_1+F_2d_2+F_3d_3$.

The displacement is the change of position, $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_{\text{final}}-\mathbf r_{\text{initial}}$, never a position vector on its own.

### Sign of the work
| Situation | $\theta$ | Work |
|---|---|---|
| Force has a component along the motion (a push forward) | acute | positive |
| Force opposes the motion (friction, gravity on the way up) | obtuse | negative |
| Force perpendicular to the motion (normal reaction, weight on level ground) | $90^\circ$ | zero |

### Work against gravity and the work-energy principle
Raising a mass $m$ through a vertical height $h$ requires work $mgh$ against gravity, and gravity does $-mgh$. The work done by the resultant force on a particle equals its change in kinetic energy:

$$
W_{\text{resultant}}=\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mu^2 \tag{2}
$$

### Work done by a variable force
When the force changes along the path, add up the small amounts of work $\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r$. If the position is a function of time, $d\mathbf r=\mathbf v\,dt$, so

$$
W=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\,dt \tag{3}
$$

with $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$ for the resultant force. Differentiate $\mathbf r$ to get $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf a$, form the scalar product $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v$, then integrate.

variantes.nom: Scalar form: force at an angle, and work on a slope
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the force and displacement are described by magnitudes, an angle or a vertical height instead of vectors.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A force of 40 N at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal drags a crate 5 m along the horizontal: $W=40\times5\times\cos60^\circ=100\ \mathrm{J}$ (the angle used is between the force and the displacement). Lifting a 5 kg block through a vertical height of 3 m needs $W=mgh=5\times9.8\times3=147\ \mathrm{J}$. On a smooth slope at angle $\alpha$, a displacement $s$ up the slope is a rise of $s\sin\alpha$, so the work done against gravity is $mg\,s\sin\alpha$.

variantes.nom: Position vector given as a function of time
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives $\mathbf r(t)$ and the mass, and asks for the work done by the resultant force over a time interval.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Take $m=3\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $\mathbf r=t^2\mathbf i+2t\mathbf j$. Then $\mathbf v=2t\mathbf i+2\mathbf j$, $\mathbf a=2\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf F=6\mathbf i$. So $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=12t$ and the work from $t=0$ to $t=3$ is $\int_0^3 12t\,dt=\left[6t^2\right]_0^3=54\ \mathrm{J}$. Check with energy: at $t=3$, $\mathbf v=6\mathbf i+2\mathbf j$ and $\frac12(3)(40)=60\ \mathrm{J}$; at $t=0$, $\mathbf v=2\mathbf j$ and $\frac12(3)(4)=6\ \mathrm{J}$; the difference is $54\ \mathrm{J}$.

sections.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf F=(2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ moves its point of application from $A$, with position vector $(\mathbf i+2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$, to $B$, with position vector $(4\mathbf i-\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$. Find the work done by the force, and the angle between the force and the displacement.

etapes.justification: The displacement is the final position minus the initial position, $\mathbf r_B-\mathbf r_A$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: $\mathbf d=(4-1)\mathbf i+(-1-2)\mathbf j+(3-0)\mathbf k=(3\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$

etapes.action: Form the scalar product $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d$.
etapes.justification: Multiply the matching components and add; the result is a scalar.

etapes.action: Attach the unit and interpret the sign.
etapes.justification: Force is in newtons and displacement in metres, so work is in joules. A positive value means the force has a component in the direction of motion.

etapes.action: Find the magnitudes of $\mathbf F$ and $\mathbf d$.
etapes.justification: Use $|\mathbf a|=\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2}$ to prepare $\cos\theta=\dfrac{W}{|\mathbf F||\mathbf d|}$.
Rearranging $W=|\mathbf F||\mathbf d|\cos\theta$ gives the cosine of the angle between the force and the displacement.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The work done by the force is $21\ \mathrm J$ and the angle between the force and the displacement is about $28.1^\circ$ (acute, so the work is positive).

items.erreur_markdown: Computing the work as $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf r_Q$ for $\mathbf F=(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j)\ \mathrm N$ with $\mathbf r_P=(\mathbf i+3\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$, $\mathbf r_Q=(4\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$, giving $12\ \mathrm J$.
items.pourquoi_faux: A position vector measures where the point is from the origin, not how far it has moved. Work depends on the change of position.
items.correction_markdown: $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_Q-\mathbf r_P=3\mathbf i+\mathbf j$, so $W=2(3)+1(1)=7\ \mathrm J$.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=(2\times3)\mathbf i+(1\times1)\mathbf j=6\mathbf i+\mathbf j$ for the same force and displacement.
items.pourquoi_faux: The scalar product of two vectors is a number, not a vector: the products of components are added, not kept separate.

items.erreur_markdown: For a 40 N force at $60^\circ$ above the horizontal and a horizontal displacement of 5 m, using $W=40\times5\times\sin60^\circ\approx173\ \mathrm J$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The work uses the component of the force along the displacement, $F\cos\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between force and displacement. With $\sin$, the component is taken perpendicular to the motion.

items.erreur_markdown: For a particle of mass 1 kg with $\mathbf r=t^3\mathbf i$, finding the work from $t=0$ to $t=1$ as $\mathbf F(1)\cdot[\mathbf r(1)-\mathbf r(0)]=6\ \mathrm J$.
items.pourquoi_faux: The force $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a=6t\mathbf i$ is not constant, so using its final value overestimates the work. The formula $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d$ holds only for a constant force.
items.correction_markdown: $W=\int_0^1 6t\times3t^2\,dt=\left[\tfrac92t^4\right]_0^1=4.5\ \mathrm J$, which equals the kinetic energy $\tfrac12(1)(3)^2=4.5\ \mathrm J$ gained.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that gravity does $+98\ \mathrm J$ of work on a 5 kg mass lifted through 2 m.
items.pourquoi_faux: Gravity acts downward while the displacement is upward, so the angle between them is $180^\circ$ and the work is negative. The work done against gravity by the lifter is positive.
items.correction_markdown: Work done by gravity: $-mgh=-5\times9.8\times2=-98\ \mathrm J$; work done by the lifting force: $+98\ \mathrm J$.

items.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf F=(2\mathbf i-3\mathbf j+\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ moves its point of application from the point with position vector $(\mathbf i+2\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$ to the point with position vector $(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j+5\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$. Find the work done by the force.
items.solution_markdown:
Displacement: $\mathbf d=(3-1)\mathbf i+(1-0)\mathbf j+(5-2)\mathbf k=(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$.

Work: $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=2(2)+(-3)(1)+1(3)=4-3+3=$ **4 J**.

items.enonce_markdown:
A block of mass 10 kg is pulled from rest a distance of 6 m up a smooth slope inclined at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal by a force of 80 N acting parallel to the slope. Take $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(a) Find the work done by the pulling force. (b) Find the work done by gravity. (c) Find the speed of the block after the 6 m.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The force is parallel to the displacement, so $W=80\times6=$ **480 J**.

(b) The block rises $6\sin30^\circ=3$ m, so gravity does $W=-mgh=-10\times9.8\times3=$ **$-294$ J**.

(c) The normal reaction is perpendicular to the motion and does no work. By the work-energy principle, $480-294=\tfrac12(10)v^2-0$, so $186=5v^2$ and $v^2=37.2$, giving $v=$ **6.10 m s$^{-1}$** (3 s.f.).

items.enonce_markdown:
A particle of mass 4 kg has position vector $\mathbf r=(t^3\mathbf i+2t^2\mathbf j)\ \mathrm m$ at time $t$ seconds.

(a) Find its velocity and acceleration at time $t$. (b) Find the resultant force. (c) Use integration to find the work done by the resultant force from $t=0$ to $t=2$. (d) Check your answer using kinetic energy.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathbf v=\dfrac{d\mathbf r}{dt}=(3t^2\mathbf i+4t\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $\mathbf a=\dfrac{d\mathbf v}{dt}=(6t\mathbf i+4\mathbf j)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

(b) $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a=(24t\mathbf i+16\mathbf j)\ \mathrm N$.

(c) $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=24t(3t^2)+16(4t)=72t^3+64t$. Then

$$
W=\int_0^2(72t^3+64t)\,dt=\left[18t^4+32t^2\right]_0^2=288+128 \tag{1}
$$

so $W=$ **416 J**.

(d) At $t=2$, $\mathbf v=12\mathbf i+8\mathbf j$ so $v^2=144+64=208$ and $\text{KE}=\tfrac12(4)(208)=416\ \mathrm J$; at $t=0$, $\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ and $\text{KE}=0$. The gain in kinetic energy is $416\ \mathrm J$, matching part (c).

items_markdown: Constant force: $W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=|\mathbf F||\mathbf d|\cos\theta$, a scalar in joules, with $\mathbf d=\mathbf r_{\text{final}}-\mathbf r_{\text{initial}}$.
Work is positive when the force helps the motion, negative when it opposes it (friction, gravity going up), and zero when perpendicular to it.
Against gravity, $W=mgh$ with $g=9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and $h$ the vertical rise; on a slope $h=s\sin\alpha$.
Work-energy principle: work done by the resultant force $=\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mu^2$.
Position vector given as $\mathbf r(t)$: differentiate to get $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf a$, take $\mathbf F=m\mathbf a$, then $W=\int\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\,dt$; check with kinetic energy.
